items.question: Will my original PDF be changed?
items.answer: Your imported PDF is kept exactly as it is. Imports are limited to 10 MiB and 100 pages. If you compose a letter with your assistant, a new document is created. You can review it before preparing its dispatch.

items.question: Can I share a password-protected PDF?
items.answer: Yes. Choose the protected-link option: the recipient receives an email without an attachment, then enters the password on Guteneo without creating an account. Hosting costs €1 per document, in addition to the email. Share the password through another channel. The link expires after the selected period and can be revoked; downloaded copies remain accessible. This option protects access and is not end-to-end encryption.

items.question: Can my assistant send without my approval?
items.answer: By default, your assistant prepares the dispatch and you approve the document, recipient, channel and cost in Guteneo. Agreement given in the conversation does not replace this approval. Expert mode is optional: only an administrator can authorise a limited, revocable delegation with an expiry date.

items.question: How do I find out the price of my dispatch?
items.answer: The price or spending limit is shown before approval, with the applicable options and taxes. The rates above are indicative. The €50 welcome credit is granted once, with no monthly renewal. If your balance does not cover the dispatch, it is blocked: no automatic charge and no negative balance.

items.question: How do I know whether my dispatch has arrived?
items.answer: Track it in your conversation and your Guteneo workspace. A transmitted fax, an email accepted by the recipient’s server and a letter handed to the postal service are distinct outcomes; they do not prove that your recipient has read the document. Delivery is shown only when confirmed. An uncertain outcome remains visible and never triggers an automatic resend.

Does European law require accessible PDFs?

The European Accessibility Act, Directive (EU) 2019/882, has applied since 28 June 2025 to certain consumer products and services, including e-commerce. Its scope has exceptions, including microenterprises providing services. It does not impose a universal requirement on every PDF.
Directive (EU) 2016/2102 also covers public-sector websites and mobile apps. Exact duties depend on the service, document, exceptions and national implementation.
Does PDF/A or a PDF/UA check prove accessibility?

PDF/A is for long-term preservation; PDF/UA concerns accessibility. These are distinct goals. veraPDF checks rules that can be automated, but reading order, meaningful alternatives and the real experience require human review. A passing report does not certify legal compliance.

The Guteneo journal tells the story of printing and document transmission, from Gutenberg to PDF.
From Gutenberg to digital, the long life of a page
Print, address, transmit: from hand-set books to documents sent in seconds, a history of changing practices and enduring needs.
From Asian printing to Gutenberg, from post to fax and email: how pages learned to multiply, travel and cross networks.
Illustration bringing together an old printing press, letters, a fax machine and a computer around printed pages.

A page seems motionless. Yet its history is one of movement: reproducing a text, taking it elsewhere, allowing someone to find it again. This history begins long before European presses. In China, the Diamond Sutra held by the British Library bears the date 11 May 868. Printed from carved wooden blocks, this scroll reveals an already sophisticated craft. It is the oldest surviving dated printed book, not the first text ever printed.

Another decisive landmark came in July 1377, when the Jikji was printed in Korea using movable metal type. According to UNESCO, its second volume is the oldest surviving evidence of this technique. Gutenberg therefore invented neither printing worldwide nor the principle of movable type. His place in this history is that of a European transformation whose scale should not obscure its Asian predecessors.
A revolution that still resembles a manuscript

In Mainz, between 1452 and 1455, Johannes Gutenberg and his collaborators produced a two-volume Bible. Movable type allowed them to compose lines, print several copies and then reuse the letters. The work changed scale: one setting could produce a series of pages. The Gutenberg Museum estimates the print run at around 180 copies, mostly on paper, with some on parchment.

The object did not break with every tradition of the handwritten book, however. Its printed text still awaited the colours and ornaments that each buyer commissioned from artisans. The copies therefore display clearly visible differences. This coexistence of mechanical reproduction and handwork explains the change better than a sudden disappearance of the old world. Innovation took hold within existing practices, trades and expectations. It transformed book production while preserving something familiar.
Sending what we write on its way

Reproducing pages is not enough to get them to their readers. Post has its own history, long predating Gutenberg: messengers, relay stations and organised services connected places and people. Postal reforms made these exchanges simpler in the nineteenth century. In England in 1840, Rowland Hill’s reform combined prepayment with a uniform domestic rate for a given weight, regardless of distance. The postage stamp embodied this new arrangement.

Borders remained a challenge. Agreements between countries multiplied, each with its own conditions and rates. On 9 October 1874, twenty-two countries signed the Treaty of Bern, founding the General Postal Union, which became the Universal Postal Union in 1878. The aim was very practical: enabling different services to exchange mail under common rules. Behind a delivered letter now stood international cooperation, as essential as paper and ink.
The fax has ancestors older than the telephone

The fax seems to belong to late twentieth-century offices. Yet its origins lie in telegraphy. In 1843, Alexander Bain patented a precursor to the fax in the United Kingdom, designed to transmit images. Bell’s telephone patent dates from 1876: the idea of reproducing a mark at a distance therefore preceded this milestone in voice transmission.

It would be misleading to imagine the familiar office machine already existing in 1843. Between a patented principle and an everyday service, machines still had to be improved, networks organised and correspondents equipped. Even so, the break was considerable: a representation of a document could now be envisaged travelling as a signal, without its sheet making the journey. The original stayed at the point of departure; its reproduction appeared at the destination.
To transmit, machines must understand each other

Technical history does not unfold only in inventors’ workshops. It also advances when different devices become able to communicate. Recommendation T.4 from the CCITT, the International Telecommunication Union’s standardisation body, provides a precise landmark: the version approved in November 1980 concerns Group 3 fax machines and document transmission. Among other things, it formalises how a page is represented and encoded.

This collective dimension deserves as much attention as the machine itself. For the sender, the action seems simple: insert a sheet, dial a number, wait. To reconstruct the page elsewhere, the equipment must share conventions. Here we meet a question already faced by postal services: how can separate systems work together? Speed becomes useful when it comes with compatibility.
Email crosses the boundary between computers

Email, too, did not emerge all at once. Before it became networked, users of shared computer systems could already leave messages for one another. In 1971, Ray Tomlinson developed mail exchange between computers on ARPANET. He chose the @ sign to separate the user’s name from the machine’s name. This milestone concerns networked mail; presenting it as the absolute invention of all electronic messaging would erase earlier work.

The Computer History Museum describes this transition as opening up a space previously limited to users of a single system. Common rules then strengthened these exchanges. In August 1982, RFC 821 described SMTP, a mail transfer protocol. Addresses, routing and inboxes use familiar vocabulary, but the journey takes place between machines. Email predates the Web and does not need a web page to exist.
The PDF carries the layout with it

Sending a message and preserving a document’s appearance are two different problems. In 1990, Adobe co-founder John Warnock set out an ambition in the Camelot project: exchanging documents faithful to their presentation, despite the variety of software and computers. Adobe launched Acrobat and the PDF format on 15 June 1993.

The page thus found a new way to travel. Its margins, images and composition could be described in a file intended for display or printing on different systems. The PDF does not, by itself, transport mail: it supplies content that can be attached, uploaded or transmitted. This separation between a document and its delivery method helps explain everyday practice. The same dossier can be viewed on screen, printed for an envelope or converted for fax transmission.

This history can be read as an accumulation of possibilities. Printing multiplies copies; postal services organise their circulation; telecommunications move signals; digital formats describe documents independently of their physical sheets. Each stage makes some operations easier without solving all the others on its own.

This reading explains why our actions remain recognisable. We prepare content, choose a recipient, decide on a delivery method and try to understand what happened. A letter, a fax and an email do not provide exactly the same experience. What they share is attention to the other end of the journey. From type assembled in a workshop to a file ready to go, a page becomes communication when it can be received, found again and understood.
Printing in Luxembourg, a history of circulation
From the first workshops to digitised newspapers, type tells the story of a country where books, languages and news cross borders.
A documented history of printing in Luxembourg: the 1598 patent, Dieudonné playing cards, newspapers, post and digital heritage.
A printing press, movable type and books before an illustrated view of Luxembourg’s rooftops and valley, engraved in blue.

Luxembourg’s history of print begins with a distinction: owning a book and making one are two different stories. The National Library of Luxembourg holds around two hundred incunabula, books printed before 1501. Their presence in its collections does not demonstrate the existence of a local workshop in the fifteenth century. Instead, it opens an enquiry into where each copy was made, who owned it and the routes it travelled.

A volume described by the BnL offers a concrete clue: sermons printed in Strasbourg by Martin Flach in 1497 bear a handwritten ownership inscription from Echternach, dated to the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century. The object thus links outside production with evidence of local ownership. For works printed before 1800, the BnL also considers printers active in the former Duchy of Luxembourg. This historical framework is not the same as the country’s present borders.

The first landmark in local printing is a patent granted on 10 April 1598 to Matthias Birthon, known as Mathias Birton at the Kulturhuef. The presentation of Luxembourg printed works by Ruhr University Bochum traces the workshop’s subsequent history. After the printer’s death six years later, his widow continued the business until 1618. She therefore belongs fully to this early history of the trade, even though the account does not give her first name.

On 18 July 1618, Hubert Reulandt, from Saint-Vith, in turn received permission to establish a printing shop. He took over the type and ornaments from Birthon’s workshop; researchers describe the transfer of the press itself as probable. His last known Luxembourg imprint dates from 1638. After a long interruption, Andreas Chevalier opened a new workshop in 1686, initially printing in Latin and French; the next German-language imprint noted in this corpus dates from 1703. The chronology thus reveals succession and breaks, rather than continuous growth from a single founding act.

Luxembourg’s printed output also took the form of objects held in a fan. In 1754, Jean Dieudonné settled in Grevenmacher and founded a playing-card factory. According to the Kulturhuef, his production was aimed chiefly at foreign markets. His descendants continued the trade until Jean-Paul Dieudonné ended production in 1880.

The surviving blocks, printed sheets and tools make this activity tangible. They remind us that printing history extends beyond books and newspapers: it also includes images repeated, cut out, distributed and used in everyday life. These cards offer another starting point for the story, at the gaming table and in export markets.
The press is also recognised by its letters

In the nineteenth century, newspapers provide a particularly rich view of print culture. The Luxemburger Wort, founded in Catholic circles in 1848 after freedom of the press was granted, is one example. Peter Gilles’s study, published on the university portal Infolux, traces its masthead from the issue of 23 March 1848. It compares the front-page nameplates over the period 1848–1980.

The result shifts our perspective: the newspaper’s name remains recognisable, but its letters change. In the nineteenth century, Fraktur alternated with a Didot, a sans-serif form and then a slab serif. An Antiqua appeared during the Nazi occupation, before the Fraktur masthead returned in 1944. Watching these changes invites us to read a page as a graphic object as well as a text. Typography helps shape its identity and can also bear traces of a political era.
After the press, the paper’s journey

Once a sheet has been produced, it still has to reach someone. Postal history adds another thread to this account. POST Luxembourg dates the creation of the Postal Administration to 1842, the issue of Luxembourg’s first postage stamp to 1852 and the country’s participation as a founding member of the Universal Postal Union to 1874. These dates concern specific institutions and services; they do not mean that all movement of mail began in 1842.

We can read these two histories together without confusing them: the workshop multiplies copies, while the postal network organises their movement. A stamp embodies a service on a small piece of paper that is itself printed. Letters and newspapers thus remind us that a document also acquires meaning through the relationship between its producer and its recipient.
A heritage kept alive through practice

At the Kulturhuef in Grevenmacher, the collection of machines gives this history a physical presence. The Linotype and Heidelberg platen press are among the highlighted exhibits. Public workshops and artist residencies also allow people to work on historic presses. Heritage remains connected to action: inking, applying pressure, discovering the impression. A finished page hides the work that made it possible; the workshop brings that work back to the foreground.
Paper also becomes a searchable archive

Another form of transmission is developing at the BnL: the digitisation of historical newspapers with optical character recognition began in 2006. The page image is accompanied by searchable text. This transformation makes research easier, but retains the original document’s difficulties. Damaged paper or a misrecognised letter can make a word invisible to the search engine even though it remains legible on the page.

The BnL developed Nautilus-OCR to improve these transcriptions. It also offers sets of public-domain newspapers as images, texts and metadata. An issue can thus be examined as a whole or its articles studied separately. The document retains an appearance, a structure and a provenance beyond the automatically extracted words.

This digital memory meets a longstanding feature of the country: several languages can share a single page. In 2023, eluxemburgensia added a language filter, while explaining the limits of automatic detection, particularly for multilingual articles. Searching, reading and returning to the original remain complementary activities. From the copy marked in Echternach to the newspaper consulted remotely, the thread of this history is one of crossings: between languages, between readers, between media.
